Propriety means correct and appropriate behavior — the kind of behavior that a society, a group, or a particular situation considers proper, fitting, and acceptable. It is about doing and saying the right thing, in the right place, in the right way, at the right time — not purely by your own private judgment, but according to the shared standards of those around you.

Think of it this way: every situation in life comes with invisible rules. At a funeral, you dress somberly and speak quietly. In a formal business meeting, you avoid crude jokes. When meeting someone's elderly grandmother for the first time, you don't use slang. When you follow these unwritten rules naturally and correctly, you are behaving with propriety.
Propriety is not the same as morality

This is one of the most important things to understand about this word. Propriety is not about being a good person in a moral or ethical sense. A person can be deeply kind and honest on the inside, and still lack propriety — perhaps they speak too bluntly at a dinner party, share a personal story that makes everyone uncomfortable, or show up to a formal event in casual clothes.

Propriety is about the surface of social life — manners, appearance, speech, and conduct as judged by others in a given situation. It is the art of fitting smoothly into the social expectations of a moment. Conversely, someone can have impeccable propriety and still be a deeply selfish or dishonest person. The two things are separate.

This is what makes the word interesting and slightly tricky: propriety's standards are not fixed or universal. They shift depending on the culture you are in, the time period you are living in, and the specific situation you find yourself in.

What is considered proper in one country may seem strange or even rude in another. Victorian-era propriety was extremely strict — rigid rules about women's dress, formal introductions before speaking to a stranger, never discussing money in polite company — rules we now find laughably stiff. And what is proper at a beach party is very different from what is proper at a court of law.

So propriety is always defined relative to a context. What the word always means, no matter the context, is this: behaving according to the accepted norms of wherever and whenever you are.

When the word is used in the plural — the proprieties — it refers to the specific rules or customs of proper behavior in a given setting, thought of one by one.

For example: "She always observed the proprieties at formal dinners." This means she followed each of the specific rules of formal dining — the right fork, the right posture, the right topics of conversation. "He ignored the proprieties of the occasion" means he broke the accepted social rules of that particular event.

A useful way to think about it: propriety (singular) is the overall quality of behaving correctly, while the proprieties (plural) are the individual items on the checklist of correct behavior.

A sense of propriety refers to an inner awareness of what is socially appropriate. Someone with a strong sense of propriety naturally knows what to do and say in various situations without being told — it is almost instinctive to them.

To behave with propriety means to conduct oneself in a proper, fitting manner. "She handled the difficult question with propriety" means she dealt with it in exactly the right, socially acceptable way.

A breach of propriety (sometimes called a violation of propriety) means breaking the rules of acceptable social behavior. This is usually something that causes embarrassment or offense, though not necessarily something illegal or deeply immoral. A crude joke at a funeral is a breach of propriety. So is a politician using an official visit for personal gain.

To observe the proprieties means to follow the accepted rules of polite or formal behavior in full. It suggests deliberate, careful attention to doing everything correctly.

Questions of propriety are situations where people debate whether something is appropriate or not — for instance, whether it is proper for a judge to publicly comment on a case they are handling.
The tone and feel of the word

Propriety has a formal, slightly old-fashioned quality to it. You would not hear it casually in everyday conversation. You are far more likely to encounter it in formal writing, literary fiction, discussions of etiquette, historical contexts (it was a very important concept in the 18th and 19th centuries), and professional or institutional settings.

When someone lacks propriety, or when a specific action is socially inappropriate, the word for that is impropriety — the direct opposite of propriety.

A few scenarios that show the full range of propriety:

At a funeral, a person who cracks loud jokes, takes selfies, and laughs boisterously is behaving without propriety. Someone who dresses somberly, speaks gently, and focuses on comforting the grieving family is showing propriety.

At a board meeting, an employee who interrupts senior colleagues, uses slang, and checks their phone repeatedly is violating propriety. An employee who listens attentively, speaks formally when addressed, and waits their turn demonstrates propriety.

In a letter of condolence, writing something dismissive like "Well, these things happen — life goes on!" would be a breach of propriety. A warm, careful, and respectful letter shows propriety in written communication.

A journalist who secretly records a private conversation for a story might be technically breaking no law, but many would argue it is still a breach of professional propriety.
One final sentence to lock it in

Propriety is the quality of behaving in a way that is considered correct, fitting, and socially acceptable for a particular situation — not by your own private standards alone, but according to the shared expectations of the people and culture around you.
